title: Precautionary principle

definition.text: An approach to new activities or technologies that might cause harm when scientific knowledge about them is still incomplete, favouring caution and review first.

facts.text: Policy makers often use it when a decision might cause harm and conclusive evidence is not yet available.
The English term is generally thought to come from the German Vorsorgeprinzip, adopted in the 1970s in response to forest decline and sea pollution.
It shifts the burden of proof: whoever proposes an activity must show it will not, or is very unlikely to, cause significant harm.
Its second core idea is that the response should be proportionate to the risk and to the cost and feasibility of acting.
One study found 14 different formulations of the principle in treaties and declarations.
EU environmental policy must be based on the precautionary principle along with prevention, fixing damage at source and polluter pays.
It is typically applied to climate change, new organisms such as GMOs, public health threats and long-term effects of new technologies.
Critics argue it is vague, self-cancelling, unscientific and an obstacle to progress.

contested_note: Supporters see it as needed caution under uncertainty, while critics call it vague, incoherent and a barrier to innovation.

definition.text: Two versions of the precautionary principle: the strong one requires regulation whenever harm is possible, the weak one only permits action without full proof.

facts.text: Strong precaution demands regulation even if the evidence is speculative and the economic costs are high, a 'no-regrets' stance that ignores cost.
The 1982 UN World Charter for Nature gave the first international recognition to the strong version.
Weak formulations allow benefits to be weighed against costs, and economic factors may justify delay.
People practise weak precaution daily, such as buying smoke detectors or wearing seatbelts.

title: Precautionary approach (Rio Principle 15)

definition.text: A softer form of the precautionary principle, set out in Principle 15 of the 1992 Rio Declaration, that takes local capabilities and costs into account.

facts.text: Principle 15 says that where serious or irreversible damage threatens, lack of full scientific certainty is no reason to postpone cost-effective preventive measures.
The United States has opposed the word 'principle' in negotiations because a principle of law is a source of law.
The Cartagena Protocol on Biosafety builds on the precautionary approach of Principle 15.

contested_note: The line between the precautionary principle and the precautionary approach is described as diffuse and sometimes controversial.

title: Precautionary dilemma

definition.text: The common objection that weak versions of the precautionary principle are trivial and strong versions are incoherent.

facts.text: Cass Sunstein argued that the weak version only states a truism.
Applying strong precaution can itself cause harm by blocking innovation and keeping current harmful technologies in use.
For example, banning nuclear plants over low-probability risks means continued reliance on fossil-fuel plants and their air-pollution deaths.

contested_note: Critics hold that no version of the principle is both useful and coherent, a view its defenders reject.

definition.text: A form of government spending that passes money from taxpayers to individuals, households or businesses to support them or encourage some activity.

facts.text: Subsidies take forms such as direct spending, tax incentives, cheap loans, price support and government-provided goods and services.
The word can also cover support from NGOs or international organizations, not only governments.
Governments may hand out direct payments in a downturn to help people pay bills and to boost economic activity.
Spending on subsidies stays high in many countries, often several percentage points of GDP.
Some governments subsidise rail and bus transport, which cut congestion and pollution compared with cars.
Many subsidies create perverse incentives and harmful unintended consequences.

definition.text: Subsidies are sorted as direct or indirect, production or consumption, and broad or narrow.

facts.text: Direct subsidies are cash outlays to a specific person or household, such as cash grants; indirect ones include tax breaks and low-interest loans.
Production subsidies help suppliers expand output by offsetting costs; consumption subsidies lower the price consumers pay.
Consumption subsidies are most common in developing countries, for basics such as food, water, electricity and education.
Broad subsidies are hard to identify and include non-monetary support; environmental externalities are the most common type.

definition.text: How a subsidy changes a market: it shifts the supply or demand curve to the right by the amount of the subsidy.

facts.text: In a competitive market, a subsidy pushes supply beyond the equilibrium quantity, creating deadweight loss.
Deadweight loss from a subsidy is the amount by which its cost exceeds its gains, and it grows with the subsidy's size.
A demand subsidy tends to raise prices, while a supply subsidy can lower them.
Subsidized goods sold abroad lower world prices, hurting producers in poorer countries and causing trade tensions.
In 2019 the OECD urged countries to use more environmental taxation and phase out agricultural subsidies and environmentally harmful tax breaks.

definition.text: Subsidies whose effects are clearly and significantly harmful both to the economy and to the environment.

facts.text: A subsidy rarely starts out perverse but can become so if it is not withdrawn after reaching its goal.
They drain government budgets away from priorities such as conservation, education and health.
They cause environmental damage such as resource overuse and pollution, and tend to benefit the rich at the expense of the poor.
They become 'locked' into society through bureaucratic roadblocks and institutional inertia, so they are hard to remove.
In 2005 US farmers received $14 billion and EU farmers $47 billion in agricultural subsidies.
Government subsidies in agriculture often fuel environmental damage, deforestation and overfishing.

definition.text: Government support for fishing, such as direct aid to fishers, loans, tax breaks, infrastructure and price support.

facts.text: In 2002 the WWF estimated that about 75% of the world's major fisheries were overexploited.
These subsidies expand fleets and catches, favouring large-scale operations over small-scale fishers.
Together they keep marine fisheries overcapitalized and overfished.

definition.text: A label stating the carbon dioxide emitted in making, transporting or disposing of a consumer product.

facts.text: The first carbon label, the Carbon Reduction Label, was introduced in the UK in 2006 by the Carbon Trust.
The Carbon Trust label required companies to commit to cutting the product's embodied carbon or lose the label.
The Swiss climatop label instead marks products at least 20% better than others in their category.
Carbon labels focus on greenhouse gas emissions rather than direct energy use.
